reviewBoundary: Three complete original senior five-of-seven plus ten-gap grammar practices. Each grammar has seven prompted and three one-word gaps. Same-author cohesion, all-candidate and form-variant review; no independent calibration.

units.title: Listening to a book and preparing a costume
units.alignmentNote: Old sources are level/family drafting references only. Final National I structure: complete five-gap seven-option insertion plus complete ten-gap grammar passage.

materials.title: A. Listening to a book and preparing a costume
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
An audiobook can make a familiar story feel new. The narrator supplies pace, emphasis and voices that a silent reader would otherwise imagine. Enjoying this version does not require treating it as the only possible way to hear the book.

Begin with a short sample. Listen for whether the voice suits you and whether you can follow changes between speakers. ____1____ A voice that sounds attractive for one minute may be tiring over several chapters.

Think about the activity you will combine with listening. A quiet journey differs from a task that requires frequent decisions. ____2____ Missing part of a scene may reflect divided attention rather than an unclear story.

Use the controls when you need them. ____3____ Returning to the start of a conversation can restore a connection that continuing at the same speed would leave unclear. Pausing is part of listening, not a failure to keep up.

If the book contains unfamiliar names, a printed list can help. ____4____ Seeing them once may make later appearances easier to recognise by ear.

Finally, allow your response to differ from a friend's. One listener may enjoy a dramatic performance while another prefers a quieter reading. ____5____ Comparing those reactions can reveal what each voice brings to the story without requiring a single winner.
candidates: A. A narrator may record different characters on separate working days.
B. Rewind a little instead of guessing when you lose the thread.
C. Personal preference plays a part in what holds your attention.
D. Those spellings can connect sounds that otherwise seem unrelated.
E. Try enough of the sample to notice the pace as well as the tone.
F. More demanding activities leave less attention for the spoken words.
G. Some libraries lend recordings through an online catalogue.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: Correct: E. Try enough of the sample to notice the pace as well as the tone. E elaborates sample testing and anticipates tiring pace. D names, B rewind, C preferences, F divided attention fit later; A recording work and G lending are not sample evaluation.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 2.
questions.explanation: Correct: F. More demanding activities leave less attention for the spoken words. F explains why concurrent decisions may interrupt comprehension. E sample/C preference/D spelling/B controls do not explain divided attention; A/G change subject.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Rewind a little instead of guessing when you lose the thread. B names rewinding and is developed by returning to a conversation. D names/C taste/E sample/F concurrent tasks do not introduce that control; A/G concern production/access.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Those spellings can connect sounds that otherwise seem unrelated. D refers to the printed unfamiliar names through Those spellings and prepares later auditory recognition. Other sentences do not refer to this list.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Personal preference plays a part in what holds your attention. C connects friends’ different preferences to comparing reactions. E/F concern testing/tasks, D/B names/controls and A/G recording/lending, not legitimate taste differences.

materials.title: B. Listening to a book and preparing a costume
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
Our drama group ____1____ (prepare) costumes for the spring show when a box of old clothes arrived. A neighbour had offered the items, but we did not assume that every piece would suit the play. We spread them out and checked the condition of each one.

There were several ____2____ (scarf), two jackets and a hat with a loose ribbon. The student ____3____ was playing the traveller tried on a grey coat. Its sleeves were too long, so our teacher folded them back temporarily before deciding whether to alter them.

I was asked ____4____ (write) a label for every item we borrowed. Some clothes would be returned to their owners after the show, while others had been donated. The distinction mattered ____5____ we needed permission before making permanent changes.

A jacket was much ____6____ (heavy) than it looked. The actor wore it during a rehearsal to check how it felt while moving. A costume could look right in a photograph and still be uncomfortable for a whole scene.

After ____7____ (discuss) the results, we chose a lighter jacket. The unused pieces ____8____ (pack) carefully and placed on a shelf. We kept the labels attached so the return arrangements would remain clear.

On opening night, I checked ____9____ (we) list once more. Every borrowed item had an owner recorded beside it. It was ____10____ useful record when we cleared the hall afterwards, because remembering a costume's colour was not the same as knowing where it should go.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with the correct form of prepare.
questions.explanation: Drama group takes singular collective was or notional plural were in the ongoing past scene. Preparing alone lacks auxiliary.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with the correct form of scarf.
questions.explanation: Several requires a plural; scarves/scarfs are both standard variants. Singular scarf is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Student is subject of was playing, so who/that. Which does not normally refer to this person; where is not a subject pronoun.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with the correct form of write.
questions.explanation: Was asked takes to write. Base/-ing/past do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Reason clause takes because/as/since. During cannot directly introduce a finite clause.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with the correct form of heavy.
questions.explanation: Much heavier compares jacket appearance and felt weight. Superlative/double comparative do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with the correct form of discuss.
questions.explanation: After discussing/having discussed both introduce completed discussion. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with the correct form of pack.
questions.explanation: Plural pieces receive packing, were/had been packed. Packed lacks auxiliary and was disagrees.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 9 with the correct form of we.
questions.explanation: Our modifies list. Subject/object/independent possessive do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 10 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Useful begins with consonant /j/, so a. Other article readings remain reviewable.

units.title: Following a word and filming a short scene
units.alignmentNote: Old sources are level/family drafting references only. Final National I structure: complete five-gap seven-option insertion plus complete ten-gap grammar passage.

materials.title: A. Following a word and filming a short scene
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Learning where a word came from can be entertaining. It can also tempt us to tell a neat story that the surviving evidence does not support. A useful account distinguishes the history that can be traced from an appealing explanation repeated without a source.

Start with the exact word and sense you are investigating. ____1____ A history of one use may not explain every other use of the same spelling.

Next, look for dated examples rather than only a claim about origins. An early printed occurrence shows that the word was in use by that date. ____2____ Someone may have spoken or written it earlier in material that has not survived.

Notice changes in meaning. A word borrowed for one object may later describe something very different. ____3____ Jumping directly from the oldest sense to today's sense can hide the steps that make the development understandable.

Treat a memorable anecdote as a lead to investigate. ____4____ If no source can be found, keep that uncertainty visible rather than improving the story until it sounds certain.

Finally, remember that an origin does not dictate every present use. ____5____ Speakers can extend, narrow or change a word's meaning. Its history enriches our understanding without acting as a permanent instruction about what it is allowed to mean.
candidates: A. Ask where the anecdote was recorded and what evidence supports it.
B. Similar spellings can carry several meanings worth separating.
C. A borrowed expression may be written in more than one alphabet.
D. That does not establish the moment when it was first invented.
E. Current meaning also depends on how a community uses the word now.
F. Look for intermediate examples that connect those different senses.
G. Dictionaries sometimes use different symbols for pronunciation.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Similar spellings can carry several meanings worth separating. B explains why the exact sense must be selected. G pronunciation/C alphabet concern form rather than distinct senses; D/F/A/E fit later evidence/history/use moves.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 2.
questions.explanation: Correct: D. That does not establish the moment when it was first invented. D limits an earliest surviving date rather than treating it as invention, developed by missing earlier records. Others do not contrast survival with invention.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: Correct: F. Look for intermediate examples that connect those different senses. F asks for intermediate uses and is reinforced by not jumping over development. D dates/A anecdote/E current practice/B separate senses do not bridge historical stages.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Ask where the anecdote was recorded and what evidence supports it. A gives a concrete source/evidence test for the anecdote. G/C merely change written form; other choices address separate stages.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: Correct: E. Current meaning also depends on how a community uses the word now. E connects present community use to semantic change. F is historical bridging, D early evidence, A source checking and G/C/B other issues, not the current-meaning basis.

materials.title: B. Following a word and filming a short scene
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
We filmed a short scene for the school language festival. Before the first rehearsal, our teacher asked us ____1____ (decide) what the audience needed to understand. We had only three minutes, so a complicated plot would leave little room for the characters to speak naturally.

The story concerned two friends ____2____ found the same lost notebook. One wanted to open it for clues; the other preferred to give it directly to a teacher. The disagreement could be shown through ordinary actions rather than a long explanation.

Several ____3____ (version) of the opening were tried. In the first, both actors spoke at once. Their words ____4____ (hear) only with difficulty on the recording, so we changed the timing instead of asking them simply to shout.

After ____5____ (watch) the trial, we moved the camera closer. It made the expressions clearer, although the actors had to stay within a smaller area. Each change solved one problem and created another choice ____6____ us to consider.

The final scene was ____7____ (short) than our original plan. We had removed a repeated explanation, not part of the action necessary to understand the ending. The teacher asked us to describe that difference ____8____ (clear) in our project notes.

We saved ____9____ (we) final script beside the video. It showed what had been planned and helped explain the changes made while filming. When the scene was shown, the audience laughed at ____10____ unexpected pause. We had left it in because it made the friends' hesitation visible without adding another sentence.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with the correct form of decide.
questions.explanation: Asked us takes to decide. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Friends is subject antecedent, who/that. Which normally nonhuman; where is not subject pronoun.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with the correct form of version.
questions.explanation: Several requires plural versions. Singular and process noun do not count alternative openings.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with the correct form of hear.
questions.explanation: Plural words receive hearing, were/could be heard. Heard alone lacks auxiliary and was disagrees.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with the correct form of watch.
questions.explanation: After watching/having watched fit completed trial viewing. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: A choice for us to consider introduces us as the infinitive’s subject. Of/from do not fit this construction.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with the correct form of short.
questions.explanation: Than requires shorter. Superlative/double comparative do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with the correct form of clear.
questions.explanation: Clearly modifies describe; clearance is a noun. Unlisted flat-adverb readings remain reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 9 with the correct form of we.
questions.explanation: Our modifies final script. Personal and independent possessive forms do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 10 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Unexpected begins with vowel sound; an. Other article readings remain reviewable.

units.title: Reading a town map and recording a shadow
units.alignmentNote: Old sources are level/family drafting references only. Final National I structure: complete five-gap seven-option insertion plus complete ten-gap grammar passage.

materials.title: A. Reading a town map and recording a shadow
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A town map selects from a complicated place. Streets, buildings and paths can be represented in many ways, depending on whom the map is intended to help. Reading it well involves asking what its symbols include and what its design leaves in the background.

Begin with the key. A thick line might identify a main road, a bus route or a walking trail. ____1____ Familiar-looking marks do not necessarily carry familiar meanings across different maps.

Check the date and the area covered. A detailed centre may fade into a simplified edge. ____2____ Beyond that edge, a blank region can mean missing coverage rather than empty land.

Notice how distance is represented. A visitor map may enlarge a crowded area so labels remain readable. ____3____ Use an appropriate scale or another source if exact travel distance matters.

Consider the intended user. A map designed for drivers may omit stairs or narrow footpaths important to a pedestrian. ____4____ Its omissions can follow its purpose without making it useless for that purpose.

Finally, compare the map with conditions on arrival. Gates close and routes change. ____5____ Treating the map as a guide to check, rather than a promise about every current detail, can make it more useful and your journey easier to adapt.
candidates: A. A useful route on paper may therefore be unavailable on the day.
B. A street can have different names at different points in its history.
C. Read what each line means on this particular map.
D. The mapmaker may choose colours that reproduce clearly in print.
E. That emphasis may distort the apparent distance between landmarks.
F. Establish where reliable detail gives way to a less complete view.
G. Look for another map if your journey depends on features it omits.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Read what each line means on this particular map. C directs the key-specific symbol interpretation and leads to different meanings across maps. D print/B old names do not decode lines; others serve later checks.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 2.
questions.explanation: Correct: F. Establish where reliable detail gives way to a less complete view. F locates transition from detailed centre to incomplete edge, supporting the warning about blank areas. E distance/C lines/G user needs/A closure do not define coverage.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: Correct: E. That emphasis may distort the apparent distance between landmarks. E refers to enlargement emphasis and explains why apparent distance may mislead. F coverage/C key/G purpose/A current closures address other limits.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: Correct: G. Look for another map if your journey depends on features it omits. G responds to missing pedestrian features and preserves the map’s driver purpose. Others do not offer a relevant alternative for omitted journey needs.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A useful route on paper may therefore be unavailable on the day. A follows changing gates/routes with the consequence that paper route may be unusable. D print/B naming history and E/F/C/G earlier considerations do not state that day-specific consequence.

materials.title: B. Reading a town map and recording a shadow
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
Our class used the school courtyard to record how a shadow changed during the day. The experiment ____1____ (begin) on a clear morning, after our teacher had checked that the chosen place would remain available. We used a fixed post rather than asking someone to stand still for hours.

A mark ____2____ (make) at the end of the shadow every thirty minutes. Beside each mark, we wrote the time. These ____3____ (record) helped us distinguish a genuine change in position from uncertainty about when an observation had been taken.

The student ____4____ notebook contained our plan noticed that the first measurement lacked a unit. We added the missing detail before continuing. A number could look precise while leaving the reader unsure what had actually been measured.

After ____5____ (compare) the morning marks, we expected the next one to fall in a similar direction. The teacher asked us to keep that expectation separate ____6____ the observation. We still needed to look, not merely copy a predicted point onto the ground.

At lunchtime, a passing cloud made the edge ____7____ (difficult) to identify than before. We noted the condition rather than inventing a sharp boundary. The measurements were later described ____8____ (careful), including the limits of our method.

We placed ____9____ (we) drawings beside the table of times. The two records supported each other, but neither was a complete account of the Sun's movement. It was ____10____ useful first investigation because it gave us both a pattern to explain and practical questions about how that pattern had been recorded.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with the correct form of begin.
questions.explanation: Past morning narrative takes began. Base and unaided -ing do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with the correct form of make.
questions.explanation: Singular mark receives making, was made. Made lacks auxiliary and were disagrees.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with the correct form of record.
questions.explanation: These requires plural records in count reference. Singular record/recording do not fit these.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Whose modifies notebook to show possession. Other relative forms do not directly determine the noun.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with the correct form of compare.
questions.explanation: After comparing/having compared both fit prior comparison. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Keep expectation separate from observation uses separate from. Of/to do not fit here.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with the correct form of difficult.
questions.explanation: Than requires more difficult. Superlative and malformed double comparative do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with the correct form of careful.
questions.explanation: Carefully modifies described; carefulness is a noun. Unlisted flat-adverb readings remain reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 9 with the correct form of we.
questions.explanation: Our modifies drawings. Personal and independent possessive forms do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 10 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Useful begins with consonant /j/, so a. Other article readings remain reviewable.
